title: Subspaces, Span & Linear Combinations (4.2)
description: 24 True/False questions covering the three-part subspace test, common gotchas (quadrants, unions of subspaces, shifted lines, degree-exactly-n polynomials, invertible matrices), and the definitions of span and linear combination. 8 pulled per attempt.

questions.prompt: A subspace W of a vector space V must contain the zero vector of V.
explanations: This is one of the three required conditions. If W doesn't contain 0, it automatically fails to be a subspace, no matter what else is true about it.

questions.prompt: A subset W of a vector space V is a subspace as long as it is closed under addition and scalar multiplication — it does not also need to contain the zero vector.
explanations: All three conditions (contains 0, closed under addition, closed under scalar multiplication) are part of the definition — none of them is optional.

questions.prompt: If W is a subspace of V, then W is itself a vector space, using the same addition and scalar multiplication as V.
explanations: This is exactly the point of the subspace test — it's a shortcut for checking all 8 vector space axioms by confirming W inherits them from V.

questions.prompt: The set W = {0} containing only the zero vector is a subspace of every vector space V.
explanations: This is called the trivial subspace — it trivially contains 0, and 0+0=0 and c·0=0 for every scalar c.

questions.prompt: A vector space V is a subspace of itself.
explanations: V trivially satisfies all three conditions with respect to itself.

questions.prompt: Every vector space has at least one subspace.
explanations: Every vector space V has at least two subspaces built in for free: the trivial subspace {0} and V itself.

questions.prompt: The first quadrant of R² — all points (x, y) with x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0 — is a subspace of R².
explanations: It contains (0,0) and is closed under addition, but it is NOT closed under scalar multiplication: (1,1) is in the quadrant, but (-1)(1,1) = (-1,-1) is not.

questions.prompt: In R², the union of the x-axis and the y-axis (all points on either axis) is a subspace.
explanations: It contains 0 and is closed under scalar multiplication, but NOT under addition: (1,0) and (0,1) are both in the union, but (1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1) is on neither axis.

questions.prompt: A line through the origin in R² is a subspace of R².
explanations: A line through the origin is exactly the span of a single nonzero vector, and spans are always subspaces.

questions.prompt: A line in R² that does NOT pass through the origin can still be a subspace of R².
explanations: A line that misses the origin can't contain the zero vector, so it fails the very first condition immediately.

questions.prompt: The set of all invertible 2×2 matrices is a subspace of M₂ₓ₂ (the vector space of all 2×2 matrices).
explanations: The zero matrix isn't invertible, so this set doesn't even contain the zero vector. It also isn't closed under addition — e.g. I and -I are both invertible, but I+(-I)=0 is not.

questions.prompt: The set of all symmetric 2×2 matrices (those with Aᵀ = A) is a subspace of M₂ₓ₂.
explanations: The zero matrix is symmetric, the sum of two symmetric matrices is symmetric, and a scalar multiple of a symmetric matrix is symmetric — all three conditions hold.

questions.prompt: In P₂, the set of polynomials p(x) with p(0) = 0 is a subspace of P₂.
explanations: The zero polynomial satisfies p(0)=0, and this condition is preserved under addition and scalar multiplication.

questions.prompt: In P₂, the set of polynomials with degree exactly 2 (nonzero leading coefficient) is a subspace of P₂.
explanations: The zero polynomial has no degree at all, so it's not in this set. Also, two degree-2 polynomials can add to something of lower degree — e.g. (x²+x) + (-x²+x) = 2x, which isn't degree 2.

questions.prompt: The solution set of a homogeneous linear system Ax = 0 is a subspace of Rⁿ.
explanations: x=0 is always a solution, and if Ax=0 and Ay=0 then A(x+y)=0 and A(cx)=0 — all three conditions check out.

questions.prompt: The solution set of a consistent nonhomogeneous system Ax = b, with b ≠ 0, is a subspace of Rⁿ.
explanations: The zero vector isn't a solution here, since A·0 = 0 ≠ b. Failing to contain 0 is enough by itself to rule this out as a subspace.

questions.prompt: A linear combination of vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₖ is any sum c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ + ⋯ + cₖvₖ for some choice of scalars c₁, …, cₖ.
explanations: This is exactly the definition of a linear combination.

questions.prompt: The span of a set of vectors S is the set of all linear combinations of vectors in S.
explanations: This is exactly the definition of span(S).

questions.prompt: The span of any nonempty set of vectors in a vector space V is always a subspace of V.
explanations: This is an important theorem: span(S) automatically contains 0 (take all coefficients 0) and is automatically closed under addition and scalar multiplication.

questions.prompt: If S = {v} is a single nonzero vector in R², then span(S) is a line through the origin.
explanations: span{v} = {cv : c is a scalar}, which traces out exactly the line through the origin in the direction of v.

questions.prompt: The span of the zero vector alone, span{0}, is the empty set.
explanations: span{0} = {0} — it's not empty, it's the trivial subspace containing just the zero vector (every scalar multiple of 0 is still 0).

questions.prompt: Every subspace of Rⁿ can be described as the span of some set of vectors.
explanations: You can always take a spanning set of the subspace itself (for instance, all of its own vectors) — every subspace equals the span of some set.

questions.prompt: A set consisting of just the zero vector, S = {0}, satisfies span(S) = {0}.
explanations: Every linear combination of just the zero vector is still the zero vector, so span{0} = {0}.

questions.prompt: If W₁ and W₂ are both subspaces of V, then their union W₁ ∪ W₂ is always a subspace of V.
explanations: The union of two subspaces need not be closed under addition — the x-axis and y-axis are each subspaces of R², but their union isn't, since (1,0)+(0,1)=(1,1) is in neither.
